Lake Vistonis bleak (Alburnus vistonicus) is a freshwater cyprinid endemic to a single lake system in northeastern Greece, where it occupies pelagic zones and undergoes a relatively compressed life cycle. During the spawning season, the gonadosomatic index (GSI) averaged 13% [GSI = 13%] when measured at a stable water temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C]. Adult body size is constrained by local environmental conditions, with the ultimate total length of wild-caught specimens rarely exceeding 21.7 cm [Li = 21.7 cm]. This asymptotic size, documented from extensive gillnet surveys across several years, suggests a growth trajectory shaped largely by the relatively warm, productive waters of Lake Vistonis, where maturation occurs before the full range of somatic growth is realized.

The onset of puberty in this species marks a distinct life-history transition, occurring at a relatively small body size compared to many other members of the genus Alburnus. Field data indicate that the total length at puberty is approximately 11.3 cm [Lp = approximately 11.3 cm], a dimension at which individuals typically begin gonadal recrudescence and enter the mature portion of the population. This value, derived from histological examination of gonadal tissue across multiple cohorts, underscores a pattern of early maturation in a shallow, warm lake environment where annual mortality pressures are moderate. The corresponding wet weight at puberty is 12.76 grams [Wwp = 12.76 grams], a body mass that reflects sufficient somatic reserves to support initial gametogenesis. Fish at this stage are particularly vulnerable to size-selective predation by piscivorous birds, yet the timing of puberty appears to balance the benefits of early reproduction against the survival costs of delayed breeding.

Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae are extremely small at the moment of eclosion, with a wet weight at birth of just 0.001 grams [Wwb = just 0.001 grams], a mass that corresponds to a pelagic egg diameter of roughly 1.25 millimeters. This diminutive size places the species among the smallest-hatching cyprinids in the region, and the lecithotrophic larvae must rely entirely on their endogenous yolk reserves during the first several days of free-swimming life. The rapid yolk absorption that follows is critical, as the point of no return is reached within a narrow window under the warm conditions typical of late spring in this lake system.

Adult body mass at the end of the growth period is modest for a fish of its ultimate length, with the ultimate wet weight reaching 97.7 grams [Wwi = 97.7 grams] among the largest individuals examined.
